women-development-s2.title: A village lending group reports (invented passage for practice)
women-development-s2.html:
From the 2026 yearly note of the Lake District Women's Savings Group, an invented lending group in Country A.

Our group lends small sums, most under 200 dollars, to women who meet each week in circles of five. No one needs land or a building as security: the circle stands behind each loan. This year 118 of our 120 borrowers repaid on time. Most bought goats, sewing machines or stock for small shops. Members tell us they now pay school fees for their daughters. Two members had to borrow from a moneylender to repay us after their shops failed, and many members sell the same goods at the same market.

sustainable-development-s1.title: A reserve office writes about visitors (invented passage for practice)
sustainable-development-s1.html:
From the 2026 visitor report of the Southern Forest Reserve, an invented protected forest in Country A.

Before the reserve opened in 2012, loggers cleared part of the forest each year. Since then, villagers who once cut trees work as guides, cooks and lodge staff, and every visitor pays a park fee that funds rangers. We allow 400 visitors a day and keep them on marked trails. Last year, however, three lodges owned by firms from the capital took most of the bookings, and some villagers say little of the money reaches them. Most visitors fly in from abroad.

items.q: The legend says each marked region sits on a coalfield. Why did early factories cluster in places like these?
options: Coal fueled the steam engines
Coalfields were where the best farmland was found
Rulers kept factories away from the coast by law
Each was a capital

items.q: At what scale of analysis does this map show early industrial regions?
options: Regional: places in several countries of Europe
Local: one neighborhood inside one single city
Global: the whole world shown at once on one map
National: one country and its many provinces

items.q: Manchester, marked A on the map, grew from a market town into a large factory city in the early 1800s. Which explanation of that growth includes every link?
options: Mills on the coalfield needed workers, so farmworkers moved in
Manchester grew larger because it was an industrial place in England
Farmworkers moved away from Manchester to farm land in colonies
Its birth rate rose sharply after its mills shut down

items.q: According to the chart, between which years did the share of workers in factories and mines first pass the share in farming?
Which statement best describes the trend the chart shows for Country A over the whole century?
options: Work shifted from farms to factories and mines
Farming and factory work both grew at the same pace
Factory work peaked in 1840 and then fell back again
Most workers in 1900 still farmed, just as in 1800

items.q: Which outcome is most likely in Country A as the chart's trend goes on?
options: Towns grow as rural people take factory jobs
Cities empty out as factory workers go back to farms
Farm output drops to zero as farmworkers leave
People spread evenly over the land

items.q: Which is a limitation of the chart for studying industrialization inside Country A?

It uses invented data, so it shows no clear trend over time
It covers too many years for a reader to see a trend

items.q: Great Britain was the first place to industrialize, in the late 1700s. Which combination best explains why?
options: New machines plus coal, iron and trade wealth
The largest population of any country in the world then
A law against farming that pushed people into towns
A warm climate that suited factory work year-round

items.q: How did the steam engine change where factories could be built?

options: Factories needed raw materials and new buyers
European factories ran short of workers and wanted farmland
Colonies had already built more factories than Europe
European governments wanted to slow their own factories

items.q: Britain industrialized in the late 1700s mainly through private mill owners. Japan began after 1868 with its government bringing in foreign machines and advisers. What does this difference show?
options: Later places could industrialize by a state-led route
Japan copied British laws and policies one by one
Japanese industry started without machines or power
Later industrializers had little need for raw materials

items.q: Which were effects of industrialization in Britain in the 1800s? Select all that apply.
options: A large urban working class that earned wages in factories
Rapid growth of mill towns, with crowded housing
A move of most people back to farms in the countryside
A sharp drop in trade with other continents
Fewer goods made, at higher prices

items.q: Put the steps of the Industrial Revolution in Britain in cause-and-effect order, first to last.
options: New machines and steam power are invented
Factories open in towns near coal
Farmworkers move to towns for factory jobs
Cities grow quickly and crowd up

items.q: An invented mill town in Country A had 20,000 people in 1800 and 140,000 people in 1850. By what percent did its population grow? (Invented data for practice.)

mistakes.why: That is the new size as a percent of the old (700%). Growth subtracts the old value first: (140,000 minus 20,000) over 20,000, times 100.
You divided by the new value. Percent change divides the change by the old value, 20,000.

items.q: Build an explanation of how the Industrial Revolution changed one city, naming the place and the scale.

specific.frame: At the ___ scale, in ___, steam mills needed many workers, so ___.
specific.model: At the local scale, in Manchester, England, steam mills needed many workers, so farmworkers moved in for wages and the city grew quickly.

scale.label: Scale of analysis
options: local
global

why.1: One city is the local scale; the global scale is the whole world.

place.label: Place
options: Manchester, England
many places in Europe

why.1: Name one real place: readers give no credit for a vague place.

effect.label: Effect
options: farmworkers moved in for wages and the city grew quickly
the city grew

why.1: "The city grew" leaves out the link: say who moved and why.

items.q: Build an explanation of why copper is smelted near the mines of northern Chile, naming the model.

specific.frame: Using ___, copper is smelted near the mines of northern Chile because ___, so ___.
specific.model: Using least cost theory, copper is smelted near the mines of northern Chile because copper ore is mostly waste rock, so shipping the smelted metal costs far less than shipping the ore.

model.label: Model
options: least cost theory
the demographic transition model

why.1: That model is about birth and death rates, not where factories locate.

cause.label: Cause
options: copper ore is mostly waste rock
Chile has many workers

why.1: Labor is a cost, but the location here is set by the ore's weight.

effect.label: Effect
options: shipping the smelted metal costs far less than shipping the ore
the copper becomes heavier

why.1: Smelting is weight-losing: the product is lighter than the ore.

items.q: Using least cost theory, place each factory where its transport costs are lowest.

slips.why: Bottling adds water, so the product gets heavier: ship it the shortest distance by locating near buyers.
A break-of-bulk point is a transfer place, not a factory to locate.

items.q: Build a statement of one limitation of GNI per capita as a measure of development.

specific.frame: GNI per capita shows ___, but it hides ___, so ___.
specific.model: GNI per capita shows the average income per person, but it hides how income is shared, so a few very rich people can make a country look better off than most of its people are.

data.label: What it shows
options: the average income per person
the health of the people

why.1: Health is in life expectancy and the HDI, not GNI per capita.

limit.label: What it hides
options: how income is shared
the size of the population

why.1: Per capita already divides by population.

effect.label: So
options: a few very rich people can make a country look better off than most of its people are
it is the best single measure

why.1: A limitation explains what goes wrong; it is not praise.

scale.label: Scale of analysis
options: local
global

somewhere poor

a seat in parliament

effect.label: So

items.q: Build a statement of one limit of Rostow's model, naming a place.

specific.frame: Rostow's model assumes ___, but in ___, ___, so the model fits poorly.
specific.model: Rostow's model assumes every country follows one Western path, but in Zambia, colonial rule built an economy around copper exports, so the model fits poorly.

model.label: Assumption
options: every country follows one Western path
death rates fall before birth rates

why.1: That is an assumption of the demographic transition model.

place.label: Place
options: Zambia
every poor country

why.1: Name one real place; a sweeping claim earns no credit.

cause.label: What happened there
options: colonial rule built an economy around copper exports
the climate stopped all industry

why.1: Climate as the sole cause is environmental determinism.

items.q: According to the table, which country has the absolute advantage in making tablets?
